Testimony in Support of
An Act to Provide One-Time Funds to Support the Construction of a Psychiatric Residential Treatment Facility for At-Risk Youth - LD 2065 January 29, 2026
Good morning, Senator Ingwersen, Representative Meyer, and honorable members of the Committee on Health and Human Services. My name is Adam Bloom-Paicopolos. I am a resident of Wells and am proud to serve as the Executive Director of the Alliance for Addiction and Mental Health Services, Maine (the Alliance). The Alliance is the statewide association representing 34 of Maine's community-based behavioral health agencies who provide mental health and substance use services to over 120,000 children, adults, and families annually. The Alliance advocates for the implementation of sound policies and evidence-based practices that serve to enhance the quality and effectiveness of our behavioral health care system.
On behalf of the Alliance, I am here today to speak in favor of LD 2065, "An Act to Provide One-time Funds to Support the Construction of a Psychiatric Residential Treatment Facility for At-risk Youth."
This $1.1 million capital investment is critical for the PRTF to come to fruition. Without this additional funding Maine still faces a glaring gap in Maine's behavioral health system for children and adolescents. We also recognize that the final fiscal note will ultimately be informed by the state's final budget negotiated with CMS as part of its Rural Health Transformation Program funding - which includes support for this PRTF.
PRTFs are secure therapeutic residences that provide non-hospital inpatient psychiatric care and treatment to youth with MaineCare coverage under the age of 21. These non-hospital settings are less restrictive than hospital settings and are a safe alternative for treating children who have a less acute psychiatric illness but still require a locked, structured residential setting due to their serious emotional disorder. Care is provided under the guidance of a physician.
The Legislature has already decided that Maine needs this PRTF, and we are grateful for the continued support of this Administration as signified by the inclusion of support for this project in its Rural Health Transformation Program application.
LD 2065 provides the last portion of capital funding necessary for this essential facility. While this is one-time funding for construction, it represents Maine's commitment to building a more comprehensive system of care for our most vulnerable youth. We know what the gap is in our service system and what is needed. We need to act.
I respectfully urge you to support LD 2065 and take this important step toward bringing Maine children home and giving them the specialized care they desperately need.

TESTIMONY OF THE MAINE MEDICAL ASSOCIATION AND THE MAINE OSTEOPATHIC ASSOCIATION

In Support Of

LD 2065

An Act to Provide One-time Funds to Support the Construction of a Psychiatric Residential

Treatment Facility for At-risk Youth

Joint Standing Committee on Health and Human Services Room 209, Cross Building, Augusta, Maine Thursday, January 29, 2026

Good Morning, Senator Ingwersen, Representative Meyer, and Members of the Joint Standing Committee on Health and Human Services. My name is Anne Sedlack, and I am the Director of Advocacy at the Maine Medical Association. I am submitting this testimony in support of LD 2065 an Act to Provide One-time Funds to Support the Construction of a Psychiatric Residential Treatment Facility for At-risk Youth, on behalf of the Maine Medical Association and Maine Osteopathic Association.

The Maine Medical Association (MMA) is a professional organization representing over 4,300 allopathic and osteopathic physicians, residents, and medical students in Maine. MMA's mission is to support Maine physicians, advance the quality of medicine in Maine, and promote the health of all Maine people. The Maine Osteopathic Association (MOA) is a professional organization representing more than 1,200 osteopathic physicians, residents, and medical students in Maine whose mission is to serve the Osteopathic profession of the State of Maine through a coordinated effort of professional education, advocacy, and member services in order to ensure the availability of quality osteopathic health care to the people of this State.

The MMA and MOA's legislative committees have united on this issue and are here today to testify in support of LD 2065.
Physicians throughout the state have notified us that our child residential treatment system is stretched too thin. These circumstances have led to children spending exorbitant amounts of time in emergency departments, being moved to out-of-state facilities, or cycling through inadequate crisis services.
Psychiatric residential treatment facilities provide 24-hour live-in care for individuals under the age of 21 who are suffering. These facilities are key to bridging the gap between

emergency care, family living, and therapy. Currently, Maine families are forced to look out of state in order to find the right facilities to care for their at-risk children, leading to painful family separations.
Our members know that forcing parents to choose between sending their children to out-of-state facilities and keeping them in homes where they do not have adequate resources is an impossible choice to face. We hope that by building a psychiatric residential treatment facility, it will allow for Maine children to get the help they deserve while remaining close to the ones they love.
Thank you for considering the thoughts of Maine's physicians, and we hope you support LD 2065.
Thank you,
Anne Sedlack, Esq., M.S.W. Director of Advocacy Maine Medical Association Email: asedlack@mainephysicians.org
10059229:
Testimony of Beth White Maine Service Employees Association, SEIU Local 1989
In Support of LD 2065, An Act to Provide One-time Funds to Support the Construction of a Psychiatric Residential Treatment Facility for At-risk Youth Sponsored by Senator Henry Ingwersen
Before the Joint Standing Committee on Health and Human Services 10am Thursday, January 29, 2026, Cross Building Room 209 and Electronically
Senator Ingwersen, Representative Meyer, and members of the Joint Standing Committee on Health and Human Services, I'm Beth White, Director of Politics & Legislation for the Maine Service Employees Association, Local 1989 of the Service Employees International Union. We are a labor union representing over 13,000 Maine workers, including workers at the Department of Health and Human Services (DHHS) and the Department of Corrections (DOC).
We're here today in support of LD 2065, which would provide one-time funding for the construction of a psychiatric residential treatment facility for at-risk youth. We want to thank the sponsor, cosponsors and members of this Committee for the work you all have been doing to address the challenges at the Office of Children and Family Services (OCFS).
As you are aware, there has been an ongoing crisis at OCFS with children being placed in hotel rooms or hospital emergency rooms for extended periods of time, mainly due to a lack of alternative placements and foster homes for them. As MSEA member Bernice "Bunny" Wermenchuk said in testimony on the budget last session, "Hoteling is not in the best interest of any child. Hoteling offers no stability, structure, or security. There is no privacy or a sense of belonging. Without a place to cook and refrigerate food, meals provide no nutritional benefits or offers no ability to learn life skills. The cost to the state to hotel for one night: 1 hotel room, roughly $25 for food and drinks for the child, overtime pay for staffing....And lastly, travel expenses to and from the hotel for the staff. And that is for 1 child in 1 county. Currently some counties are hoteling multiple children for multiple nights. Hoteling and ED covering is the number one cause of burnout amongst OCFS staff along with high case load."
This legislation will help address the issues of children being placed in hotels and emergency departments, which often stems from the lack of long-term placements and solutions for children. Currently, our members are concerned about the wait times between when some children are discharged from acute care, such as a hospital emergency department, to when a bed is available in a Psychiatric Residential Treatment Facility (PRTF). There simply are not

enough PRTF beds to meet current needs, which exacerbates the situation. Passing and funding this legislation to build a new Psychiatric Residential Treatment Facility in Maine would make significant progress on this issue.
While we are supportive of this legislation and thankful for its introduction, it's important to note that more needs to be done in the immediate term to address the hoteling crisis. Frontline workers have consistently indicated a solution needs to be developed which addresses the trauma of having children placed in hotels due to lack of resource homes. They have identified two additional needs outside of building a new PRTF:
1. The need to increase the number of enhanced therapeutic foster homes for children with behavioral health needs. There are many examples that could demonstrate this need; one is when a child has severe behavioral health needs, including non-verbal and self-harm behaviors. In these cases, there is concern about the wait time between when the child is discharged from acute care, such as a hospital emergency department, to when a bed is available in a Psychiatric Residential Treatment Facility (PRTF). While addressing the need for a new PRTF would help significantly, more licensed intensive therapeutic homes are needed for these interim situations between acute care discharge and long term PRTF placements. More needs to be done to increase the number of licensed intensive therapeutic homes for children in these situations.
2. The need for placement of children waiting for permanent placements in a residence (such as a bridge home) which offers structure for education, nutrition, socialization, etc. Children can be discharged from an acute treatment facility (generally a hospital) and their condition is considered stable and not needing treatment beyond outpatient therapy and possible community support. However, these children may remain without a residence, as a home is not available. A hotel setting is not structured for a child's emotional growth as there is no dedicated staff.
That being said, we strongly support LD 2065 and our members are eager to see more details about the proposed facility and how it would be operated. We would encourage this committee to pass this legislation and advocate for its funding.
At the bottom of this document, I have also included "Our vision for Child and Family Services", which was written by our members in 2019 and updated in 2023. It includes numerous recommendations for improvements at OCFS. I'm also more than happy to connect you all with workers at OCFS if desired.

Thank you and I would be happy to answer any questions.
Our vision for Child and Family Services, updated 2023 All children deserve safe childhoods. We do this work because we care deeply about Maine children. We are determined to protect them, support them and build families that also can protect and support them. We believe that to do this effectively, serious changes need to be made to Maine DHHS policies, practices and programs. We must recruit and retain staff to stabilize quality public services for Maine children and families. The people who do the frontline work must be empowered to shape the policies and program they implement each day.
Recommendations from frontline workers on how we get there
Provide the necessary resources for support programming, including public health nurses and housing, mental health and addiction resources. Caseworkers need these types of services fully resourced and staffed so Maine families can get the support they need.
OCFS caseworkers and support staff are first responders, similar to firefighters and police personnel. Resources have been focused on assessing the immediate evidence of abuse and neglect versus the promotion of healthy family dynamics. The focus needs to be on prevention, including economic factors, housing, physical and mental health services, education and other community supports.
In simplistic terms, a call to intake regarding neglect because a family is living in a shanty or car, is not poor parenting; it is an economic and affordable housing issue. There also is a lack of awareness by the public of the devastating impact of a government investigation on a family. This is evident by the predictability of the cycle of increased reports of abuse and neglect to the intake units just prior to school breaks - time periods where children are perceived as potentially at risk because schools and other similar providers are not in a position to have a consistent "eyes on the situation." During those time periods, mandated reporters or others may believe they are providing a safeguard but there is no corresponding increase in OCFS staffing for that vacation week or summer break.
Reduce caseloads to manageable caseloads that match the national standard of no more than 12 cases per caseworker in the field. This will provide the necessary time with every child and capacity for family plans.
Every child should be counted as one case. While Governor Mills has added 70 new staff positions, a significant number of those positions remain unfilled. With an everrevolving door for the hiring of caseworkers, the question becomes: Why is the OCFS unable to keep child protective caseworkers?

In discussion with child protective workers in the field (intake is a separate unit), individual caseloads consistently average over 20 cases and sometimes as high as 30 or more.
Hire more administrative support staff, allowing caseworkers to have the time they need to focus on casework.
Customer Service Representative IIs are considered support staff. When an average person thinks of administrative support staff, the visualization probably is of a person handling the phone calls, filing of paperwork, updating information in databases, etc., not someone who is in direct contact with parents and children. OCFS utilizes Customer Service Representatives to transport children, monitor children during parental visitations and sit with children in hotels and emergency rooms. Community Care Workers' workloads and responsibilities have increased commensurate with the child protective caseworkers' inability to keep up with their increased caseloads. With the decrease in services normally provided by community agencies, OCFS would not function without the Community Care Workers and Customer Services Representatives.
End forced overtime, taking work home and missing work breaks and lunch breaks, all of which are leading to burnout and stress.
Despite the implementation of the overnight CES unit, A majority of OCFS employees (CRA-IIs, Community Care workers, Child Protective Caseworkers and Supervisors) are still facing mandatory overtime, missed lunch breaks, etc. Documentation remains an issue, resulting in missed breaks and working after hours.
Ensure the safety of staff as they work in the field. Similar to other first responders such as police and fire personnel, always being ready to deal with a crisis is hard on an individual's mental and physical health.
OCFS caseworkers and other staff are often in potentially violent situations with no law enforcement backup.
Due to the lack of therapeutic setting for children with severe mental illness, OCFS staff often are in hotel situations with limited support. Multiple OCFS staff have been treated for assault by children.
Provide the technology that truly functions to meet the needs of the Maine Office of Child and Family Services workers and efficiently integrates into their work. This means investing in the right technology and the right training, not just the least expensive.
While caseworkers applaud the development of a new system, and caseworkers appreciate there was to be a learning curve, Katahdin has not lived up to expectations and in many ways has created more barriers than those experienced with the old system, MacWIS. The Katahdin system does not provide a smooth narrative of a case, a

major obstacle for anyone "picking up" a case as there is no simplified method to access a chronological linear narrative. There is no search function. Instead of reducing the information needed, there are too many screens requiring a check box and, in all honesty, not enough lines in the screen to complete the information required. Basically, Katahdin has clunkier hyperlinks and is less efficient than the old system. As a caseworker is only allowed to read three lines at a time and cannot make the window bigger, the overall result is Katahdin has made it difficult to make timely and accurate decisions. Documentation is difficult in Katahdin as the system is more compartmentalized with more walls. Often depending on the circumstances, accessing one window to pull information for a second window often deletes the information entered. Another issue is the algorithm known as single decision making. The algorithm determines the weight of a reported statement; human experience and knowledge is excluded.
There has been no open and honest review of Katahdin by a panel of caseworkers, supervisors and others who were not a part of the original design. As with any project, those involved with the original development can be biased if changes are suggested by others. Policies and practices continue to be top-down driven, with little to no acceptance of feedback from supervisors or frontline caseworkers.
Reduce unneeded or duplicative paperwork, including making case plans more accessible and usable for families. (See difficulties with Katahdin.)
Give front-line workers a voice in policies, practices and programs so they can meaningfully participate in developing and implementing them.
Policies continue to be top-down driven, with little to no acceptance of feedback from supervisors or frontline caseworkers.
The use of algorithms such as single decision making have multiple drawbacks. Despite the implementation of SDM, the number of tragedies in the past five years has not decreased. Algorithms create more investigations, which delay the documentation of caseworkers' current caseloads, creating a spirally effect: there's not enough time in eight hours to do the investigation, so documentation is frequently done after hours to meet deadlines. A review of deadlines for documentation is needed to determine if a deadline is valid and consistent with national social work ethics and standards ensuring the well-being of the child.
Establish a night shift for coverage across Maine DHHS districts.
Due to hiring delays, the complete rollout of the Children's Emergency Services (CES) Unit is too early for an assessment. Currently many districts are still experiencing having to cover overnights and holidays. There is a concern regarding funding for the CES Unit.

Is there enough staff? Similar to a firehouse situation, there needs to be a recognition that a CES Unit is mainly there for a crisis call.
Intake Unit - This unit experiences a large volume of calls; it's essential to always have the staffing levels necessary to handle a large volume of calls.
Reassess the foster parent certification process, training and support to better build and support Maine's network of foster parents.
Improvements continue to be needed in this area, more so for residential care of children diagnosed with severe autism, trauma syndrome or brain injury. Too often children are languishing in hotels or emergency rooms due to lack of therapeutic placements.

Testimony in Support of LD 2065
An Act to Provide One-time Funds to Support the Construction of a Psychiatric
Residential Treatment Facility for At-risk Youth
Chair Ingwerson, Chair Meyer, and members of the Health and Human Services
Committee:
My name is Bob Staples. I am the President of the Brett M. Staples Brain Disorder Awareness Coalition, and I am here today in strong support of LD
2065.
This bill addresses a reality Maine can no longer work around: we do not have
enough appropriate, therapeutic residential capacity for youth with serious
brain disorders who are already at risk.
When care does not exist at the right level, at the right time, children fall through
gaps that quickly become lifelong consequences. Families are left cycling through emergency rooms. Youth are placed far from home, sent out of state, or held in settings that were never designed to treat complex brain-based conditions. And far too often, the first "placement" becomes the juvenile justice system--not because of criminal intent, but because care failed to show up.
LD 2065 is not about expanding institutionalization. It is about building the
missing middle--a therapeutic residential option for youth who are too ill to be safely treated at home, but who do not belong in hospitals, detention, or adult
systems.
This funding is one-time, targeted, and practical. It invests in infrastructure that
Maine has lacked for years, even as need has grown. And it recognizes something critical: early, appropriate treatment changes trajectories. When serious brain
disorders are addressed in adolescence with stability, continuity, and clinical expertise, outcomes improve--not just for the child, but for families, schools, and communities.
From a systems perspective, this investment also makes fiscal sense. Residential
treatment capacity reduces repeated emergency department boarding, law enforcement involvement, hospital readmissions, and costly out-of-state placements. Inaction is not neutral--it is expensive, disruptive, and harmful.

I would urge the committee to ensure that any facility supported under this bill
emphasizes:
~ Developmentally appropriate, trauma-informed care
' Family engagement and continuity
' Coordination with education and community-based services
' And clear pathways back to the least restrictive, most supportive
environment possible
This bill sends an important message to Maine families: your children are worth
building for.
LD 2065 does not claim to solve everything. But it takes a meaningful, responsible
step toward a system that treats youth brain health as urgent, real, and deserving of investment--before crisis becomes destiny.
I respectfully urge the committee to support LD 2065.
Thank you for your time and your commitment to Maine's children and families.

Senator Ingwersen, Representative Meyer, and honorable members of the

Thank you for the opportunity to speak.
My name is Dr. Deirdre Burns, I am a pediatrician practicing in York
County and have practiced in Cumberland County in the past. I am speaking
to you in support of LD 2065 because I personally have witnessed the
distress of families seeking inpatient psychiatric placement for their
children. These are children in dire situations who are not safe to return home, and may wait days or weeks seeking a bed. I personally have cared
for children waiting in the Emergency Department for an inpatient
psychiatric bed.

Imagine a child in your life in crisis, desperately in need of high-level
psychiatric care, and made to Wait days and days in a windowless room or in
a windowless hallway waiting for that help. While waiting, these children
receive supportive care from doctors, nurses, and social workers, who want
nothing more than for that child to be in a therapeutic setting where they can heal and make progress. These inpatient psychiatric beds are elusive and scarce, creating uncertainty as to when or if the child will be lucky enough to be placed. Hours and hours of case management time is spent making the
7 calls to various facilities, getting on thewaitlists, and callingback every W W ._
day to let them know we still want the bed, and again calling to find out if we got the bed.
One argument against this bill is that children should be at home and not in a residential facility. I see parents who would love nothing more than to be able to have their child at home participating in intensive outpatient services,
however their child is a threat to the safety of themselves, their family members, or the community. I have witnessed the heartbreak of parents
who are unable to provide a round-the-clock safety watch for their child because at some point parents have to sleep or earn a living for their family. I have seen parents who have to put the safety and well-being of all children in the home first. I have spoken to parents who are physically overpowered by a child who is a threat to themself and others. I have seen parents who have secured the funding for an in-home caregiver but cannot find anyone to fill the position.
A good day in Maine will be a day when We can't fill all of our pediatric
inpatient psychiatric beds. I don't anticipate that day coming soon. Until
then, we need more resources for these children who have the most need.
I ask that you vote "Ought to Pass" on LD 2065 and approve funding to
construct a new psychiatric residential treatment facility for at-risk youth.
Deirdre Burns, MD, l\/IPH, FAAP

Dear Senator Ingwersen, Representative Meyer, and honorable members of the Committee on Health and Human Services,
My name is Emma Freeman. I grew up in Scarborough and am a pediatric resident physician based in Portland. My co-resident Calvin Schaffer of Cape Elizabeth and I are writing today on behalf of the Maine Chapter of the American Academy of Pediatrics to express our support for LD 2065 "An Act to Provide One-time Funds to Support the Construction of a Psychiatric Residential Treatment Facility for At-risk Youth."
LD 2065 seeks to provide one-time funds to support the construction of a psychiatric residential treatment facility for at-risk youth under 21 years of age. This will increase access to necessary psychiatric care for children, adolescents, and young adults who have been unable to receive life-saving treatment in their home state.
In Maine, more than 12,000 youths have serious thoughts of suicide each year. In 2024, more than 1,900 youths visited an emergency department for suicidal thoughts or attempts. Patients with a multitude of psychiatric concerns, including suicide attempts, are often deemed unsafe to leave the hospital and are recommended to await placement in an inpatient psychiatric facility. Recent data shows that the average days spent on waitlists for behavioral health care can range from 135-372 days. This results in patients boarding in the emergency department or being admitted to the pediatrics unit, which are not equipped to provide adequate care to such patients, while awaiting placement. Unfortunately, due to the lack of inpatient psychiatric care in Maine, patients are often awaiting placement at an out-of-state facility. From 2018 to 2024, up to 85 Maine youths were living in out-of-state residential facilities.
As pediatric physicians in Maine, we have seen the impacts of these prolonged admissions on the healthcare system, providers, and the patients themselves. In my personal experience, without these facilities in Maine, we have had to leave the state to receive adequate training in caring for this population, which is becoming increasingly needed. I have seen multiple patients require weeks to months of inpatient hospital admission while awaiting placement in a residential facility. Our emergency departments and pediatric units do not have the resources, training, or staff to appropriately care for patients requiring intensive psychiatric care. This has resulted in accidental and non-accidental harm to staff, use of restraints in patients with unsafe behaviors, delayed effective care for these patients, and in providers often being pulled away from other patients, whose recovery is also significantly disrupted by frequent behavioral concerns on the unit. This is counterproductive to the treatment and recovery of all our pediatric patients. An established residential psychiatric facility would reduce the strain on our healthcare systems, allow families to be near their children as

they receive care, and most importantly be the best way to help these children and adolescents get the care that they need as quickly as possible.
Supporting LD 2065 means supporting access to necessary healthcare for all of Maine's youth. Thank you for your consideration.
Sincerely, Emma Freeman, MD Member, Maine Chapter of the American Academy of Pediatrics
Calvin Schaffer, MD Board Member, Maine Chapter of the American Academy of Pediatrics

Testimony ofSenator Henry Ingwersen introducing
LD 2065, An Act to Provide One-time Funds to Support the Construction of a
Psychiatric Residential Treatment Facility for At-risk Youth Before the Joint Standing Committee on Health and Human Services
Thursday, January 29, 2026
Good morning, Representative Meyer, and fellow colleagues on the Committee on Health and Human Services. As you know, I am Senator Henry Ingwersen, and I represent Senate District
32, which includes Arundel, Biddeford, Dayton, Hollis, and Lyman. Today, I am very pleased to
introduce my bill LD 2065, "An Act to Provide One-time Funds to Support the Construction
of a Psychiatric Residential Treatment Facility for At-risk Youth."
LD 2065 aims to fill an anticipated funding gap needed to complete construction of Maine's first
psychiatric residential treatment facility, serving at-risk youth under 21 years old. Construction
will be centered around renovating an existing building rather than building new -- saving
additional costs.
With over 70 Maine kids placed out of state, over 100 more waiting to be sent out of state, and dozens languishing in emergency rooms with nowhere to go, getting this facility built will ensure families stay together through their treatment journey. It will also spare the State from paying millions to send kids awav from their families for treatment.
While the financial savings to the State are important, I would be remiss if I did not mention my
serious concerns about the safety and well-being of Maine kids receiving treatment in some of
these out-of-state facilities. In 2024, the Bangor Daily News reported on residential treatment
facilities across the country: These facilities were the subject of federal investigation into their
abuse and neglect. As one example, the report raised concerns about a pair of Acadia Health Care facilities in Arkansas, which Maine approved to serve kids in 2018.`

Senator Ingwersen, Representative Meyer, and members of the Health and Human Services Committee,

My name is John McAnuff, and I am Sweetser's CFO. I am here today in support of LD 2065 and to express Sweetser's interest in partnering with the State to expand in-state psychiatric residential treatment capacity.

As you know, Maine currently lacks psychiatric residential treatment facility, or PRTF, capacity for youth with the most acute behavioral health needs. When appropriate in-state care is unavailable, children often languish in hospital emergency departments or are placed far from home, sometimes out of state. These options are disruptive for families and significantly more expensive for the State.

Sweetser has extensive experience operating intensive residential and psychiatric services. That experience has taught us two things: first, there is a clear clinical need for a PRTF in Maine; and second, these facilities are expensive to build, not because they are elaborate, but because they must be safe.

Youth served in a PRTF present higher risks related to elopement, self-harm, and harm to

others. As a result, the building itself becomes part of the treatment and safety plan.

Construction costs are driven by requirements such as:

�

Ligature- and tamper-resistant fixtures throughout resident areas

�

Complex access control and egress systems, including secure entry vestibules and

remotely controlled exits

�

Continuous monitoring and security systems, including specialized anti-climb fencing for

outdoor spaces

�

Reinforced interior construction designed to withstand damage while protecting

residents and staff

In addition, these facilities require infrastructure enhancements, including upgraded electrical service with full generator backup, specialized ventilation and cooling systems because operable windows are unsafe, fire protection upgrades, and full ADA accessibility. Many components also require specialized installation methods, which significantly increases labor costs.
Sweetser has been intentional about cost containment. This project reuses an existing building on our campus rather than pursuing new construction, which would likely exceed ten million dollars. We are retaining usable systems, selecting modest finishes, and making design choices that reduce cost wherever safety allows. Even so, the clinical and regulatory requirements of a PRTF create unavoidable capital expense.
LD 2065 is important because it recognizes that these kinds of costs are a major barrier to expanding PRTF capacity. Without state partnership, nonprofit providers cannot assume this level of financial risk, and these facilities will not be built.
Sweetser is interested in working collaboratively with the State to develop a PRTF that keeps children closer to home, reduces reliance on emergency departments and out-of-state placements, and fits within Maine's broader continuum of care. We view this as a partnership that must balance clinical quality, safety, and long-term sustainability.
LD 2065 is a thoughtful, targeted investment in Maine's children and in Maine-based solutions. I respectfully urge the Committee to support this bill.
Thank you for your time, and I would be happy to answer any questions.
John McAnuff Chief Financial Officer

time funding to support the construction of a Psychiatric Residential Treatment Facility (PRTF)
for at-risk youth.
The PRTF will be the only facility of its kind in Maine--providing the safety of an inpatient setting within a residential environment, reducing stigma, and supporting a smoother transition back
home for children served in this setting. An 8,000 square foot, 16-bed facility, the unit is staffed
with a full-time Medical Director and Clinical Director providing 24/7 psychiatric, nursing, and clinical coverage with crisis staff, CNAs, and Behavioral Health Professionals. Children will spend six to nine months receiving the right level of care at the right time, close to their families and communities.
No longer will our children be sent to facilities in Georgia or Arkansas. No longer will they remain in inpatient units or emergency departments for months while awaiting appropriate care. The PRTF will typically serve children ages 10-18 who require a secure setting for their own safety and the safety of others. These young people may experience suicidal behavior, aggression, attempts to run away, or other highly dangerous behaviors. They may have traumarelated diagnoses, mood or psychotic disorders, or personality disorders.

jIII-7
This facility will serve youth and families in every corner of Maine, from all 16 counties. Treatment is highly structured and intensive, designed for youth with the most severe psychiatric illnesses. Services will also include care for co-occurring substance use disorders, youth with problem sexualized behaviors, and children with secondary developmental disabilities. In addition to safety and stabilization, treatment will focus on facilitating a successful transition back home.
PRTFs ensure the highest level of quality, safety, and regulatory `compliance. The facility will be accredited by the Council on Accreditation (COA), comply with federal Conditions of Participation under the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS), and be state licensed--each requiring rigorous standards and measurable outcomes.
As we work to see this project through to completion, cost-saving ideas such as reducing the facility from 16 to 8 beds were explored. Ultimately, we found this would not produce a
meaningful outcome. Most expenses are fixed and driven by safety, regulatory, and licensing requirements, like others have mentioned---not by bed count. The same life safety systems, HVAC, security, emergency power, and clinical support spaces are required regardless of the unit's size. Downsizing would significantly reduce capacity, increase the cost per bed, and provide
only limited savings.

as possible.

continuum for children and adolescents.
Maine continues to face a severe shortage of in~state psychiatric residential treatment facility (PRTF) beds for youth under the age of 2l with complex behavioral health, psychiatric, and intellectual and developmental disability needs. As a result, the State has been forced to place children in out-of-state residential treatment facilities, often hundreds of miles away from their families, schools, communities and care coordinators. frequently result in poorer outcomes for children who need stability, connection and trauma-
informed care close to home.

Department of Health and Human Services was directed to implement secure children's psychiatric

Re: LD 2065 - An Act to Provide One-Time Funds to Support the Construction of a Psychiatric Residential Treatment Facility for At-Risk Youth

Senator Ingwersen, Representative Meyer and Members of the Joint Standing Committee on Health and Human Services:

Thank you for the opportunity to provide comment on LD 2065, An Act to Provide One-Time Funds to Support the Construction of a Psychiatric Residential Treatment Facility for At-Risk Youth.

This bill provides $1.1 million in one-time funding to support construction of Maine's first Psychiatric Residential Treatment Facility (PRTF) to provide services to at-risk youth under 21 years of age. PRTFs are non-hospital-based facilities that provide intensive inpatient psychiatric care, including active treatment, intensive psychiatric monitoring, rehabilitative individual, group, and family therapies, and medical supervision 24 hours a day, seven days a week. These facilities are designed for young people whose clinical needs cannot be met through lower levels of care such as residential treatment, therapeutic foster care, or community-based services, but who do not need inpatient hospitalization. There are no PRTFs in Maine, and currently youth with PRTF-level needs are referred to out-of-state services.

The Department has worked hard over the last several years to support the development of a PRTF in Maine. Since 2017, The Office of Behavioral Health (OBH) and the Office of MaineCare Services (OMS) have worked in partnership to develop and implement a reimbursement rate for PRTF level of care in Maine. In 2024, Governor Mills signed LD 2214 (P.L. 2023, c. 643) into law, which established $2 million in start-up funding to support the development of a PRTF. OBH subsequently posted a Request for Application (RFA) and in December 2024, Sweetser was the successful applicant and was awarded the contract to construct and operate the PRTF. However, there have been changes in material costs since their RFA proposal was submitted as construction cost estimates have increased significantly.

To better understand the costs, OBH engaged with Sweetser and learned that original cost estimations were significantly below the actual cost of standing up a 16-bed PRTF. Further, changes in material costs since the initial estimate have further increased the current cost estimates.

The Department is committed to exploring all potential sources of funding in collaboration with Sweetser to support the PRTF's development. OBH is also engaged in cost containment strategy discussions with Sweetser. In addition to the State funds, Sweetser is making its own investment to support the construction.
This facility will serve to strengthen the behavioral health care system for youth in Maine and provide greater access to more intensive psychiatric services for young people, rather than relying on out-of-state providers for this level of care, moving youth farther away from their natural supports and communities.
The Department and Administration are committed to being good partners in the development of this service and appreciate the opportunity to continue engaging with Sweetser and the Legislature as we work toward this shared goal. Please feel free to contact me if you have any questions during your deliberation of this bill.
Sincerely,
Sarah Squirrell, MS Director Office of Behavioral Health Maine Department of Health and Human Services
